title: The city he built
hookLine: a pool, a bazaar and a sangat: tradition says Guru Ram Das built a place for ordinary life to be holy
last: LONGING FOR DARSAN IS PART OF THE ROAD.

lines: OUT OF THE GATE, INTO THE STREET.
cards: Step out of the gate of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, and you're not in a quiet garden. You're in the street. Shops, carts, the smell of frying, someone selling bangles, someone haggling over cloth.
The Guru's house and a busy market sit side by side, and the crowd doesn't seem to find that strange. Sikh tradition says it was planned that way, from the start, by the Guru who began the city.

teach.h: A POOL, A BAZAAR, A SANGAT.
teach.b: Earlier on this path we heard about the pool itself, the pool of nectar at Amritsar. Today, look at what grew around it. Tradition says Guru Ram Das didn't only dig a pool.
He invited traders and craftspeople to come and settle, open shops and build a bazaar beside it.

So the town tradition calls Ramdaspur, after him, had three things in one place: a pool to wash in, a market to work in, and a sangat to sing with. That's an idea, not just a town plan. Look back over these days.
The Gursikh's morning: rise, bathe, remember. After the morning: work, sitting and standing, with the Name. Blessing others: help someone else remember.

teach.h: THE WEEK'S SALOK, BUILT IN BRICK.
teach.b: The city is that same salok, built in brick. The bath is the pool. The work is the bazaar.
The others are the sangat. Holiness isn't kept in a separate place you visit now and then; it's laid out next to the shop.
His son, Guru Arjan, later praised the town in a salok, paraphrased: I have seen every place, and none is like you. The Creator himself founded you. Ramdaspur is thick with people, beyond compare.
Notice what he praises: not empty silence, but a crowded town, full of buying and selling, with the Name sung in the middle of it.

teach.h: THE MARKET IS NOT OUTSIDE IT.
teach.b: Not that the market is perfect.
That the market is not outside the reach of the Name.

how: Pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar walk through the old bazaars around it on their way in and out, and Sikhs remember Guru Ram Das as the Guru who began the city.

games.q: what does “the city he built” mean?
o: a walled fortress raised to guard the Guru's family
a quiet retreat built far from trade and markets
Ramdaspur: a pool, a bazaar and a sangat together

games.q: the city and the week: tap the pairs.
p: the bath of the Gursikh's morning
the town that carried his name

s: tradition says Guru Ram Das kept the market far away from the pool
tradition says he invited traders and craftspeople to settle beside it.
Guru Arjan praised Ramdaspur as crowded and beyond compare
his salok: none is like you; thick with people, beyond compare.

games.q: you're beginning a town around a sacred pool. tradition says Guru Ram Das did what?
o: kept it quiet, with no shops nearby.
invited traders and craftspeople to settle beside it.
allowed only pilgrims to live there.
games.why: tradition says he invited traders and craftspeople, so the pool, the bazaar and the sangat grew up together.

practice: Walk in your mind through the store or street where you'll next shop, the lights, the noise, the line at the counter, a little slower than usual, feeling your feet and noticing the faces of the people working there.
At the counter, let one breath be a remembering, with Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: The city he built. Tradition says Guru Ram Das gathered a pool, a bazaar and a sangat in one town, Ramdaspur, now Amritsar. Today's word.

orig.note: Ramdaspur, the town of Ram Das: the name Guru Arjan uses for the city in his salok.

carryVoice: Your line: holy in the market. The person across the counter is part of the city too. That's the week.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Mahala 5, Ang 1362 (I have seen every place, none is like you; the Creator founded you; Ramdaspur is thick with people, beyond compare)
